articles.title_orig: How Trump is hoping to use an Asia trip to reassert his authority
articles.title_zh: How Trump is hoping to use an Asia trip to reassert his authority
articles.content_orig:
It’s a time-tested tradition: Presidents looking to reassert authority and escape political gloom head overseas for a global pick-me-up.
Ever since 1982, when Ronald Reagan traded a recession, 11% unemployment and Democrats’ 26-seat pickup for a five-day swing through Latin America, Air Force One has been leaving political upheaval behind in its contrail.
President Donald Trump will attempt to follow suit this week with a long-planned trip through Asia, punctuated Thursday by an unprecedented three-way meeting with his authoritarian counterparts from China and Russia — a splashy show of geopolitical theater alongside men whose power in their own countries goes mostly unchallenged.
Comparisons with a newly constrained US leader may be unavoidable.
The sharp rebuke Trump faced from voters this month was quickly clocked by his foreign counterparts, all watching closely for signs of fading political capital and early-onset lame-duck status. He’ll be joined on the trip by Elon Musk, whose $445 million in political spending failed to deliver Republican majorities.
“Foreign policy and presidential trips are something only the president can do. There is pomp and circumstance. There’s a focus on it,” said Edgard Kagan, a former US ambassador to Malaysia who is now senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington. “This is a way in which you start changing the narrative, and remind people that, you know, the president is still the president.”
It’s not the only complication on Trump’s plate. The scandal involving Jensen Huang’s high-powered AI chips and affair with an alleged Chinese spy will loom over the US president’s visit to Shenzhen, the gleaming hub of China’s tech industry, even though Trump’s aides insist it wouldn’t dominate the journey.
Trump doesn’t intend to raise the spying matter with Chinese leader Xi Jinping, with whom he will meet for the fourth time in just over a year, American officials have previously told CNN. Officials said they also did not expect the two men to discuss the newly revived debate inside the administration over how to further restrict high-powered chips from going to China .
“It’s probably not something we’re going to read the Chinese in on at the moment,” one senior US official said.
Never particularly enthusiastic about grueling trips through far-flung time zones, Trump departs for the Philippines Monday after shaking up his West Wing leadership and facing calls even from some allies to fire members of his Cabinet, including the secretaries of Commerce and Defense. An air travel meltdown before he left — which Trump did not address publicly for days — also raised new questions about his mindset and focus heading into the trip.
At two leaders summits — the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) in Manila and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) in Shenzhen — Trump will look to counter the narrative of his declining power by announcing new commercial deals and asserting American presence in a region that for decades has suffered from Washington’s inattention.
Like his most recent predecessors, Trump has found the “pivot to Asia” an elusive concept. His second term became bogged down by a war in the Middle East, the same region that kept George W. Bush, Barack Obama and Joe Biden from fully turning American foreign policy toward the Pacific.
Trump has spent the past year working to cultivate deeper ties Xi. And he’s been seeking new trade deals, with plans to sign an agreement with Thailand this week, White House officials said.
Yet the Iran war, along with Trump’s so-far futile efforts to end the war in Ukraine , continue to dominate his foreign policy agenda. Both are likely to hang over his talks this week in Asia, where fuel prices have spiked due to the conflicts.
So, too, will Democrats’ stateside victories lead to questions of just how much Trump has left to offer. His two signature foreign policy initiatives — global tariffs and the Iran war — led to price increases that propelled voter anger toward him and Republicans. Democrats have vowed to limit his authorities on both, challenging the long-held adage that a president has a freer hand on foreign matters.
A foreign trip has long been a way to drive home that point while also escaping Washington as the opposition prepares to assume power. Michael Deaver, an image-maker to Reagan, is credited with inventing the tactic when he arranged the Latin America trip in 1982.
Nearly every president since then has replicated the idea. Bill Clinton made a trip to the Philippines in November 1994 after Republicans swept control of Congress for the first time in decades. George W. Bush was in Vietnam a few weeks after the GOP lost Congress in 2006. Barack Obama headed to Asia in 2010 and 2014 after midterm routs. And Trump himself made a somewhat desultory visit to France in 2017 after the GOP lost its majority in the House.
“I’ve been with presidents immediately after midterm, both wins and losses, and it’s always important,” Kagan said. “It’s something that reminds the nation, it reminds foreign observers, that this is very much the president’s bailiwick.”
For Trump, that means appearing in a joint setting with powerful men to discuss the world’s affairs. For some, the meeting between Trump, Xi and Russian leader Vladimir Putin carries unpleasant echoes of the 1945 conference in the Crimean resort of Yalta, where Stalin, Churchill and an extremely ill Franklin D. Roosevelt carved up the postwar world into western and eastern spheres of influence.
Putin originally proposed the three-party summit as a venue to discuss the Ukraine war, where fraught issues of borders and sovereignty loom over nascent peace talks.
Trump’s aides insist Thursday’s meeting is nothing of the sort, and say Ukraine won’t even be on the agenda. Instead, Trump hopes to open discussions on nuclear weapons with two leaders he’s worked hard to cultivate. The last nuclear arms treaty between the US and Russia — which each have an estimated 5,000 warheads — expired in February. China, meanwhile, has been rapidly building its arsenal to more than 600 warheads but shows little interest in joining a pact.
China’s ‘miracle city’ that no US president has visited (yet)
A US official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said expectations were low for a major breakthrough, describing the talks instead as a starting point.
“It’s time for China to sort of step up to the adult table, if you will, and have adult conversations about adult things,” the official said.
Xi had initially appeared skeptical of hosting the meeting, officials said, concerned it could overshadow the APEC summit and his attempts to showcase a rising China. But on Monday China’s foreign ministry billed it as meeting of “groundbreaking significance,” with spokesperson Mao Ning saying “such efforts would will help stabilize the global situation.”
Trump, who sometimes says he envies authoritarians who rule as they wish, signed on quickly.

A photo shows NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang with a woman confirmed by a Reuters source to be Alice Huang in Taipei, Taiwan released on June 7, 2024. Photo: Reuters
Alice Huang, a former executive of a Singapore-based AI computing company, is at the center of a suspected Chinese espionage scandal after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang acknowledged an extramarital affair.
Why it matters: The investigation raises questions about whether Chinese intelligence sought access to Nvidia's technology and CEO through Alice Huang as the U.S. and China compete in the AI race.
Driving the news: Over the weekend, Jensen Huang admitted in a letter to Nvidia employees that he had a romantic relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.
Context: Little is known about Alice Huang. She has lead a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed International, a cloud computing and data center operator that became a multibillion-dollar Nvidia customer.
Read more about Alice Huang and Megaspeed below.
Zoom in: Huang, also known as Huang Le, is a Chinese citizen with a reported background in journalism and finance.
Zoom out: The New York Times reports that China's Ministry of State Security recruited Alice Huang to seek information about Jensen Huang and influence his feelings about selling AI chips to Chinese firms.
Alice Huang is a former executive of Megaspeed International, which rents out computing power from advanced Nvidia processors, giving customers power to run AI systems without owning chips.
In November 2023, Megaspeed was bought by a company called Swiftdata . Alice Huang and another director, Cang Yang, soon resigned from the company.
Employees told The Wall Street Journal that Alice Huang continued leading the business after resigning.
By the numbers: Megaspeed became an official Nvidia Cloud Partner in 2023, per Bloomberg , and purchased more than $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over roughly two years, per AP .
Follow the money: Megaspeed's balance sheet ballooned from $33 million at the end of 2023 to nearly $3 billion a year later, according to corporate records examined by Culper, a short seller with a financial interest in Nvidia's decline.
More recently, in early 2025, Alice Huang and business partner Kang Wei told investors they had "no problem securing GPUs" and touted Alibaba as a customer for a new data center project, according to the Financial Times .
State of play: U.S. authorities, including the Commerce Department and Justice Department, have investigated whether Megaspeed helped Chinese companies obtain advanced Nvidia processors and whether that violated  export-control restrictions.
What's next: Three Republican House committee chairs have requested a closed-door briefing with Jensen Huang on Nov. 18 about his interactions with Alice Huang and how Nvidia protects itself against foreign threats.

articles.title_orig: Accounting student’s AI cheating sparks South Korean exam furore
articles.title_zh: Accounting student’s AI cheating sparks South Korean exam furore
articles.content_orig:
South Korea will inspect all glasses worn by students taking its national college entrance exam this week, after the top scorer on another notoriously difficult test confessed he used AI to cheat, shaking confidence in the country’s strict examination process.
The cheating scandal prompted Prime Minister Han Sung-sook to call officials to a meeting on Monday, where the country’s education ministry was ordered to ensure test takers hand in their smart devices before exams.
Education minister Choi Kyo-jin told parliament there would be “a thorough inspection of all glasses in each test session to ensure a fair and safe testing environment.” Smart glasses have been added to a list of items prohibited inside the testing room, he said, adding that the consequences of cheating using smart devices could include criminal punishment.
This Thursday, around 550,000 students are expected to sit the country’s infamous College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT) , an arduous eight-hour exam that is seen as a barometer for future success and social status in hyper-competitive South Korea.
Each year the test brings the country to a standstill, with flights banned from taking off or landing during the half-hour-long listening comprehension section to ensure there are no distractions.
The changes to exam rules come one day after the top scoring student in the country’s accounting exam confessed to cheating, following months of scrutiny over his suspiciously high score.
In a video published online Sunday, the student said he had cheated using a miniature camera, his phone and AI, adding he had confessed to Seoul police about the fraud.
“I cheated on the tax accountant exam. I sincerely apologize for causing damage to a lot of people,” he said in the video.
He referenced the upcoming college entrance exam, warning “if there is someone thinking of cheating like I did, I’m going to tell the investigators everything, so I hope you don’t think that you won’t get caught.”
Students have found ways to cheat on tests since the dawn of time, but the rise of AI has made deception slicker and more sophisticated. Smart glasses with integrated AI engines, built-in cameras, microphones, speakers and sensors have become tools for cheating.
While old-fashioned cheating may have required craning your neck for a quick peek at your neighbor’s answers, a test taker wearing AI glasses can simply glance at a question and have the answer fed back to them in a matter of seconds.
Once reserved for tech nerds, the devices are quickly moving into the mainstream. US tech giant Meta launched its first AI-enabled glasses with Ray-Ban in late 2023 , and has since released several new versions. Last year alone, more than seven million pairs were sold.
The new technology has become especially problematic in East Asia’s test-obsessed societies, where students have turned to smart glasses and AI glasses to get an upper hand, forcing governments to take strict measures.
Earlier this year in South Korea, two students taking an exam to assess their English language skills — the results of which are often used to make hiring decisions — were caught using smart glasses.
In Taiwan, a student sitting for an entrance exam for a top medical school was discovered wearing smart glasses after proctors noticed the student staring oddly at the test, leading to an inspection that revealed the frame was emitting heat.
For China’s grueling annual college entrance exam in June – which more than 10 million hopefuls take each year – authorities required screening of all glasses.
John Liu contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Eisenkot says Netanyahu ‘cannot remain’ after alleged election interference by aide
articles.title_zh: Eisenkot says Netanyahu ‘cannot remain’ after alleged election interference by aide
articles.content_orig:
Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has said Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu cannot “remain at the helm of government for even one more minute” amid reports alleging Netanyahu’s office engaged in electoral interference.
Eisenkot, tasked with forming Israel’s new government , launched a scathing attack on his rival on Sunday, just a few hours after representatives of the two men met to discuss the possible formation of a national unity government .
“The conduct of outgoing Prime Minister Netanyahu and his inner circle poses a tangible, direct and immediate threat to Israeli democracy,” Eisenkot wrote on X.
Israeli broadcaster Channel 12 published a report earlier on Sunday alleging Netanyahu’s chief of staff, Ido Norden, lodged a complaint with the police commissioner’s office against members of the United Arab List (Ra’am) party on the eve of Israel’s October 27 election .
Norden reportedly directed police officers to an alleged intelligence source who was a former employee of Netanyahu’s office.
Based on information from the source, about 14 police officers raided the homes of three Ra’am members without a warrant and arrested them on suspicion of bribery to incentivise voting, according to Channel 12.
Netanyahu subsequently launched a campaign against Arab-led parties throughout election day. After they won a record 19 seats, he made unproven accusations of electoral fraud.
The three men were released after police determined the information from the purported intelligence source was unfounded.
The Channel 12 report also alleged that David Zini, the head of Israel’s internal intelligence agency Shin Bet, requested the attorney general’s office to wiretap five Palestinian-Israeli Knesset members on election day over suspected election interference, but the request was later rejected.
“I call for an immediate investigation into the affair and for the police and the Shin Bet to immediately clarify the details that have been published,” said Eisenkot, a former army chief.
Netanyahu’s Likud party called Eisenkot’s statement “outrageous incitement” against the prime minister.
On Friday, Eisenkot accused Netanyahu of fuelling a “racist and violent” campaign against Palestinian citizens of Israel during the elections to cling to power.
Netanyahu renewed his appeal to Eisenkot to form a unity government on Saturday, but the opposition leader called the plea a “bluff”.
However, Eisenkot had confirmed talks between his Yashar party and the Likud party over the proposal for a shared government.
Neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot’s bloc has yet secured the 61 seats needed to form a government.

The open road has been calling to drivers since the days of the Ford Model T. We also know this: no Model T generations featured USB connectivity or auxiliary ports. Vehicles have come a long way in the last century-plus, and platforms like Apple CarPlay and Android Auto have made it even easier to enjoy music streaming, messaging, and navigation apps — all without touching your phone. But an infotainment platform — be it Apple, Android, or other — is nothing without the hardware and accessories that support it. Unfortunately, should your phone die while en route to a destination, you'll be locked out of most infotainment features.
That said, there are plenty of USB chargers you can keep in your car, and some of the best ones are made by Belkin . Even if your phone interfaces wirelessly with CarPlay or Android, you'll still need a wired or wireless charger to replenish battery life. Belkin not only keeps your phone juiced though, it also has several devices that are tailor-made for cars, trucks, and SUVs. In fact, it has so many options that we thought it'd be best to whittle them down. Here's our list of the four best Belkin accessories to keep in your vehicle. There's a lot to get into, so let's kick things off with our first pick: the Belkin Magnetic Wireless Car Dash Mount.
A wireless charger should be safe and reliable, and the $48 Belkin Magnetic Wireless Car Dash Mount checks both of those boxes. This is a Qi2-certified charger that delivers up to 15 watts to a compatible phone, which includes most modern iOS and Android devices. In the box, you'll find a 27-watt DC adapter and a 3.3-foot USB-C cable to power the device. Dashboard mounts can be preferable over vent-clipped accessories, too; a good bump in the road or cold temperatures can cause the latter to unclamp.
This Belkin mount has an aluminum alloy body built for heat dissipation, and the silicone pad that grabs your phone is great for scratch resistance. You can easily switch between portrait and landscape orientations. The charger works with MagSafe cases, but it should also work well for numerous Pixelsnap and Belkin cases up to 3 millimeters thick, according to the manufacturer.
Belkin also provides specific instructions for installation: Wipe down the part of your dashboard you'll be mounting to, then wait about 20 minutes for the area to dry. It takes up to 48 hours for the gel adhesive to fully set, so make sure to build in some time before any big road trips.
Three of the four chargers we'll be discussing are powered by your vehicle's DC port, and the $20 Belkin Retractable Car Charger (30 watts) is one of our favorites. The charger features a tethered 2.3-foot USB-C cable that retracts when needed to prevent excess wire from hugging your gear shift or center console. The actual connector uses a magnetized casing, too, so it stays secured to the adapter when it's not in use.
The USB-C delivers up to 30 watts when used by itself, and up to 15 watts when the USB-A port is used simultaneously. The USB-C is also PD 3.1-certified and uses Programmable Power Supply (PPS) technology; this allows the adapter to dynamically adjust voltage in real time to provide more precise power for your tech. This makes the charger ideal for Samsung Galaxy phones and other fast-charging mobile gear. We're also glad to see an eight-point defense system (Belkin SmartProtect) that protects against thermal and electrical anomalies.
Do keep in mind that, when used solo, the USB-A only delivers up to 18 watts. Belkin also doesn't provide a USB-A cable, so you'll need to make sure you have one on hand (or purchase one) if you want to charge a second device. Lastly, for clarity, we should mention that the PD 3.1 certification only applies to the USB-C connector.
At first glance, the $25 Belkin 4-Port USB Power Extender may not look like much of an auto accessory, but don't let appearances fool you. Consider this a full-on charging station, complete with USB-C and USB-A connectivity. Power-wise, the specs are respectable; both USB-C ports deliver up to 15 watts maximum, and you can expect 12 watts max from each USB-A. The extender isn't powered by a DC adapter, though; it uses a tethered USB-C wire that's just over 6.5 feet long (make sure your car has a USB-C port!).
This charger has enough give to make it to a backseat area. There's also an integrated clip if you want to hook the device on a seat pocket, or if you'd like to lasso up whatever cord length you don't need. Unfortunately, this isn't a PD-certified charger, but you'll still be able to connect iPhones and Android devices that support fast-charging, but you won't get anything beyond 15 watts out of the two USB-C ports.
This may come as no surprise, but Belkin doesn't provide any USB cables in the box — just the charger itself. Like the other Belkin products we've covered, though, the USB Power Extender is covered by a two-year warranty. And if you end up purchasing a different adapter down the road, the 4-port charging station makes for a great desktop companion.
USB-A may be on its way to becoming a legacy port at this point, but there are still plenty of devices that use this connection for charging purposes. The $20 Belkin BoostCharge Dual USB-A Car Charger (24 watts) is a budget-friendly addition to most vehicles, and delivers up to 12 watts maximum across both of its USB-A ports. There's no USB-C or PD certification to speak of, but if you're just trying to recharge an older smartphone, tablet, or pair of wireless earbuds, the BoostCharge has got you covered.
We like the fact that Belkin thought to include an LED status indicator to confirm the adapter is receiving power. The charger is backed by a two-year limited warranty, as well as Belkin's $2,500 Connected Equipment failsafe; should a phone or other device end up defective as a result of using the charger, Belkin steps in (here are the exact terms and conditions). While the adapter is a great price, you'll need to provide your own USB-A cables; you can also add one or two to your Belkin transaction.
Measuring 2.9 inches long and 1 inch wide, the BoostCharge Dual is easy to tuck away in a glovebox or into a piece of luggage if you're packing it for travel. It's not the best Belkin charger ever made, but it's a solid investment for a wide array of gadgets.
Belkin has an massive lineup of chargers and cables to choose from, but our main goal was to home in on the products you can keep in a vehicle year-round, without worrying about the temperature. We also wanted to highlight devices that were tailor-made for charging phones, tablets, earbuds, and other types of travel-friendly tech .
All our shopping links are from Belkin's site, but you may also come across these four items on Amazon or at stores like Best Buy, Walmart, and Target. (The lowest-rated product on Amazon — the Belkin 4-Port USB Power Extender — still earned 3.9 out of 5 stars.)

articles.title_orig: Yemeni forces' retreat leaves Houthis in control of key Red Sea waterway
articles.title_zh: Yemeni forces' retreat leaves Houthis in control of key Red Sea waterway
articles.content_orig:
Yemeni pro-government forces backed by Saudi Arabia have said they are withdrawing from an area overlooking the strategically important Bab al-Mandab Strait, leaving it under the control of the Iran-backed Houthi movement.
Yemen's military said it was redeploying troops from the key shipping gateway at the southern end of the Red Sea to defend its interim capital, Aden.
The shift ends a weeks-long offensive to try to secure the area near the waterway after the Houthis seized it in a surprise offensive in September, squeezing global oil exports and prompting thousands to flee.
Houthi-run media reported later on Sunday the group had taken control of the territory. Saudi Arabia has not commented.
Pro-government forces said they had "secured" the strait in early October as they sought to retake crucial ground from the Houthis, who said they had captured areas including Perim Island at the mouth of the strait and the strategic port city of Mokha a month prior.
But the Saudi-backed forces fighting on behalf of Yemen's internationally recognised government said on Sunday they were withdrawing to reinforce troops elsewhere, with the southern city of Aden a "priority".
The Reuters news agency reported a Southern Armed Forces statement which said troops were being withdrawn "from Dhubab Airport and the Bab al-Mandab area".
It said the decision had been made with the aim of "strengthening the front lines and addressing existing threats".
The Houthis said they posed no threat to international shipping passing through the waterway when they captured it, but that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.
However, the seizure contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz.
Saudi Arabia responded with hundreds of air strikes, while the Houthis launched hundreds of drones and missiles at its cities and infrastructure.
The UN has estimated that nearly 330,000 people have been displaced in Yemen as the fighting has since escalated. Hundreds of people are reported to have been killed.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from its capital Sanaa.
The conflict escalated in 2015, after a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.
A four-year informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

articles.title_orig: In the Philippines, Trump Checks In With an Ally Resisting Chinese Aggression
articles.title_zh: In the Philippines, Trump Checks In With an Ally Resisting Chinese Aggression
articles.content_orig:
Council on Foreign Relations
Fresh off the midterm elections, President Donald Trump will travel to Asia between November 16 and 19. He will first travel to Manila, where he will attend the U.S.-Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Special Summit and hold bilateral meetings, and then travel to Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders’ summit and to meet with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and possibly also Russian President Vladimir Putin.
In neither place is he likely to receive a warm reception, though some Asian leaders are holding out hope that the coming change of majority in Congress could prompt shifts in the White House’s Asia policy, making it slightly more deferential. Trump’s second-term Asia policy has been broadly unpopular across the region, particularly its focus on tariffs against allies and partners, along with reductions to defense support. Visits this year by Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth have drawn angry responses.
The White House’s current agenda for the trip is ambitious. For one, Trump will try to get regional states to sign on to Pax Silica , the U.S.-led coalition designed to foster collaboration on export controls and investment monitoring on issues such as chips, artificial intelligence (AI), critical minerals, and data centers. Although Pax Silica is not openly stated as an effort to prevent China from obtaining the most sophisticated chips or producing the most advanced AI models, it is effectively an attempt to achieve these goals. The administration could also attempt to get Southeast Asian states to commit to buying entire AI stacks from U.S. suppliers. The White House could further announce new trade deals with Vietnam and possibly Thailand during the trip.
In China, Trump will want to come away from his meeting with Xi with a few promises, such as actually creating a hotline on AI issues, which the two countries have already agreed to set up, and a further extension of the bilateral trade truce and the truce on rare-earth exports. There also remains the possibility of a Trump-Xi-Putin summit on the sidelines of APEC regarding the Iran war, Ukraine, and other issues.
In reality, however, the trip is unlikely to produce major gains for the White House, and it could even be rebuffed in its modest goals. It could be difficult for Trump to get much cooperation on Pax Silica, for example, given turmoil at U.S. AI companies such as Nvidia , the White House’s previously blasé attitude toward AI regulation, and the growing importance in places such as Malaysia of creating data centers and cloud computing for Chinese companies. Five Southeast Asian states already have joined the China-led World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, a new multilateral body created by Beijing, supposedly designed to facilitate AI cooperation and to serve as a clear alternative to U.S. ideas on AI.
It also will be challenging to convince anyone in the region to buy the full U.S. AI stack. After all, China’s open models are cheaper and already attracting huge numbers of customers across Asia and the world. Even many U.S. companies are abandoning U.S. AI models for Chinese ones. (China’s Kimi K3 is about 40 percent cheaper than top American AI models and can nearly match their capability as well.) The CEO of Airbnb, for instance, has said that the company prefers fast-and-cheap Chinese models, and Coinbase , DoorDash , and many other U.S. companies are reportedly also using Chinese models.
Meanwhile, even if Trump meets with Xi and Putin, he will soon be facing a different Congress, one that would almost surely oppose this trilateral summit and any results from it. The idea of working with Xi and Putin is unpopular not only among Democrats but also among many Republican lawmakers, who are likely to be less inhibited in Trump’s last two years and, in many cases, remain strong supporters of Ukraine’s side in the Russia-Ukraine war. The American public also dislikes Russia, with 85 percent viewing the country very or somewhat unfavorably.
Taiwan similarly enjoys significant bipartisan congressional support. According to several congressional staffers, there could be enough support, now that the midterms are over, to push through an already-appropriated $14 billion arms sale to the island, even overriding a possible veto by Trump, regardless of what Trump tells Xi while in Shenzhen.
As for trade deals with Thailand and Vietnam, even if they are announced, they will still be little more than frameworks. Southeast Asia has little reason to trust that the White House will follow through on the nitty-gritty of trade deals, and not swing back toward more punitive approaches. After all, a deal that the United States made last year with Malaysia has still not really gone into effect, nor has a potential deal with Indonesia. And Vietnam believes that, in negotiations with the United States over a trade deal, it has already promised as much as it can, and yet is still being pushed to give more—too much, in the minds of Vietnamese officials I have spoken with in recent months.
The fact that Trump has not publicly suggested he will change policy course after the midterms—as exemplified by his retention of Defense Secretary Hegseth and choice of hard-liner Stephen Miller as chief of staff—makes Southeast Asian leaders even warier. Already hit repeatedly by tariffs, Asian leaders know all too well that the U.S. president retains the authority to set tariff policy, and that, once he does, it will be difficult for Congress or even the courts to stop him, at least in the short term.
Any “wins” that come out of the meeting with Xi are likely to be modest as well. Even if the two sides extend the truce on export controls, China is still stalling on allowing rare earths out of the country, so the United States is gaining little from Beijing’s promises; the United States is still desperately short of rare earths, and is even looking in unlikely places such as Myanmar, which the United States is trying to engage despite its horrendous rights record and ongoing civil war. Xi knows that Beijing has extensive leverage over the White House—on rare earths, on the Iran war, and on many other exports—and likely will push Trump to make even clearer statements than he did in prior summits regarding Taiwan, such as openly stating that he is against Taiwanese independence. (As noted above, Trump already has delayed the $14 billion in arms sales to Taiwan and, unlike prior U.S. presidents, treated the island as a bargaining chip in U.S.-China relations.) Trump, who has taken a soft approach toward China in the past year, could well bend and agree to make the statement Xi demands.
In the past two months, China has stepped up its aggressive actions in the South China Sea, including buzzing Philippine aircraft with fighter jets, ramming Philippine boats, and preventing the Philippines from resupplying its forces on the grounded BRP Sierra Madre at Second Thomas Shoal, a move Beijing has not used in years. Regional states such as the Philippines will be looking for clearer U.S. security guarantees, which they are unlikely to get, as the United States focuses on the Middle East and the Western Hemisphere.
As I noted in a recent article for World Politics Review, even Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., the most pro-U.S. leader in Southeast Asia, has become bitterly disappointed with what he has received in return for his backing of most U.S. policies. The White House has reduced freedom of navigation patrols in the South China Sea from the levels of prior administrations and is unlikely to promise Marcos Jr. that it will increase them; such patrols are important deterrents to Chinese actions against Philippine and Vietnamese vessels, planes, and forces in the sea.

articles.content_orig:
As the peace process struggles on and air strikes continue, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's government is preparing for two important gatherings this week -- a meeting of the so-called Ramstein Group followed by a Coalition of the Willing session, both coming as Russia shows no signs of compromise to end the war.
"There will be a Ramstein meeting -- and it must deliver results," Zelenskyy said in his November 15 nightly video address, referring the Ukraine Defense Contact Group gathering in Brussels set for November 17.
"This will send a strong signal -- a signal to Russia that Ukraine will not be left without support," Zelenskyy added.
Ukraine Says Starshield Restrictions Persist, Hampering Drone Defenses
Informally known as the Ramstein Group, the effort coordinates military support for Ukraine among Western allies. The upcoming meeting will be led by the defense ministers of Germany and Britain.
The Ukrainian leader said Kyiv's priorities are to bolster the country's air defenses, including the acquisition of additional Patriot missiles and systems and National Advanced Antiaircraft Missile Systems (NASAMS).
"The Russian ballistic missile threat remains very serious, and we have intelligence indicating that new strikes are being prepared," Zelenskyy said.
Ukraine has been struggling to defend its cities from Russia's jet-propelled drones capable of flying nearly twice as fast as older models and has sought speedier delivery of more sophisticated Western defensive weapons.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine is also preparing for a gathering in Berlin of the Coalition of the Willing, calling it "an important meeting that could be historic."
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, French President Emmanuel Macron, and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham will lead the gathering of the coalition, an informal grouping formed in early 2025 by countries pledging to aid Kyiv and potentially participate in a multinational peace force should a cease-fire be reached.
Merz said that more than 20 heads of state and government are expected. "Our goal is to achieve two things: first, to secure funding for Ukraine's defense for 2027 and, second, to reach a unified position regarding upcoming peace talks."
Zelenskyy said that "we have a chance to establish a truly strong and united European position for the negotiations."
"We are also preparing a review of the work of the existing coalitions supporting Ukraine -- which ones are truly fulfilling their tasks and which ones remain empty shells, to be honest. We will work to give them substance."
Russia, Ukraine Trade Air Attacks As US-Led Talks Fail To Break Diplomatic Deadlock
The Coalition on November 9 launched its first military exercise aimed at supporting the potential postwar era in Ukraine.
Nearly 3,000 troops from 11 countries are involved in the maneuvers designed to test ways of sustaining the peace after a cease-fire to end the war is successfully negotiated.
The exercise, led by France and Britain, is taking place in Poland, in airspace above Romania, and in the western Black Sea and is due to run until November 22.
Moscow sharply criticized the exercise, accusing the grouping of preparing for war with Russia.
On the ground, Russia and Ukraine continued to trade air attacks, days after a flurry of diplomatic activity mediated by the US yielded no breakthrough in efforts to bring peace closer.
A Russian strike on Dnipro on November 16 killed at least one person and injured three others, while another attack hit a critical industrial facility in Ukraine's west-central Vinnytsia region. Russian drone attacks also targeted energy facilities in the Cherkasy region of central Ukraine, leaving some consumers without electricity.
In his nightly video address on November 15, Zelenskyy warned that the Russian ballistic missile threat remained very serious, with intelligence indicating that preparations for new strikes were underway.
Meanwhile, Russian-installed Crimean authorities reported a strike on the Kerch Bridge, which links the occupied Ukrainian peninsula with mainland Russia, on the morning of November 16, prompting traffic restrictions.
Nearly 600 drones targeted the Moscow region overnight, with 191 intercepted near Moscow, Mayor Sergei Sobyanin claimed in a Telegram post on November 16.
A separate drone attack also reportedly sparked a fire near two oil depots in the southern Russian city of Azov, according to monitoring Telegram channels.
Speaking about Ukraine's long-range strikes targeting Russian energy facilities, Zelenskyy said Ukraine had disabled more than 55 percent of Russia's oil refining capacity.
"This is our justified response to Russia's refusal to de-escalate and its strikes on Ukraine's energy infrastructure," he added.
Zelenskyy said on X that Russian forces attacked at least nine regions on November 15, targeting energy, civilian, and railway infrastructure in some of them and injuring at least 16 people.
Also on the ground, Britain's Prince Harry met with soldiers wounded in action during a previously unannounced two-day visit to Ukraine, his fourth trip to the country since Russia's February 2022 full-scale invasion.
"You're going to ⁠win the war and then ‌you're going to be set up for success," he told a conference for medics organized by Superhumans, a specialist clinic for those injured in war.
He took part in events on November 14-15 in the western city of Lviv. His comments were only reportable on November 15 after he had left Ukraine for security reasons.

articles.title_orig: ASEAN, China fall short of agreeing on South China Sea code
articles.title_zh: ASEAN, China fall short of agreeing on South China Sea code
articles.content_orig:
China and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) have failed to conclude long-running negotiations on a code of conduct for the South China Sea during meetings in Manila, despite tentative agreement on about 80 percent of a draft, the Philippines’ foreign minister said.
“There is no conclusion yet,” Theresa Lazaro told reporters at the ASEAN summit on Sunday, adding that several key issues remain unresolved, including whether the code would be legally binding.
“The ASEAN countries plus China have also different views on how things are,” she added.
ASEAN and Beijing have been working on a code ⁠of conduct in the South China Sea, where they have overlapping claims, for more than two decades. The Philippines, as the current chair of the 11-nation association, had pledged to speed up the process and reach a deal by the end of this year.
Lazaro said she still hoped the code could be concluded under Singapore’s auspices, as the city-state takes over as chair next year.
Southeast Asian nations want the code to reflect international law, which some of them accuse China of ignoring. Beijing insists its actions have been lawful and professional.
China has laid claim to most of the South China Sea, clashing with the exclusive economic zones ⁠of Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines and Vietnam, making a functional code essential to keeping tensions from escalating and managing maritime encounters.
An international arbitration tribunal ruled in 2016 that China’s sweeping claims have no basis under international law, a decision Beijing rejects.
China and the Philippines, in particular, have faced off in a series of maritime confrontations in recent years.
The Philippines accuses Chinese ships of repeated ⁠aggressive actions inside its exclusive economic zone, including dangerous manoeuvres, firing water cannons and ⁠disrupting resupply missions. China accuses the Philippines of intruding on its territory.
Tensions escalated after Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr took office in 2022. Months of harsh words between the two countries over the sea preceded this weekend’s meetings.
Separately, ASEAN extended a ban on Myanmar’s leader attending the bloc’s annual summits, saying the country failed to comply with a 2021 peace plan.
ASEAN leaders also decried Myanmar’s military and armed groups for continuing to attack civilians in the country’s long-running civil war.
Under the ban, Myanmar can be represented only by lower-level career diplomats, including at the summit in Manila. Myanmar was due to hold ASEAN’s rotating chair this year, but because of the civil strife, the role passed to the Philippines.
The stern rebuke followed a review of progress on the Five-Point Consensus for Myanmar, approved by ASEAN in April 2021 in a bid to ease the violence that erupted after Myanmar’s military seized power from the democratically elected government of Nobel laureate Aung San Suu Kyi in February that year.
The military coup triggered widespread pro-democracy protests that were brutally quashed, leading to armed resistance and a civil war that has spread over much of the country.
In Manila, ASEAN leaders expressed “deep concern” over insufficient progress in implementing the plan and urged all parties to “stop targeted attacks against civilians and civilian infrastructure”.
There are “still certain bombings and displacement of Myanmar people, so step-by-step, we give it to them, how they’re going to tackle this issue, and we’ll monitor that,” said Lazaro, who is also ASEAN’s current special envoy to Myanmar.
Myanmar leader Min Aung Hlaing, the former chief of the military, has made official visits to several ASEAN member states since assuming the presidency after elections in December and January, widely seen as having been rigged.
ASEAN has not discouraged those visits, but its leaders have emphasised that the peace plan remains “the main reference for addressing the political crisis in Myanmar”.

articles.title_orig: Women prosecuted for abortions hail ‘historic day’ after receiving pardon
articles.title_zh: Women prosecuted for abortions hail ‘historic day’ after receiving pardon
articles.content_orig:
Calls for government to issue formal apology to those investigated after ending pregnancies in England and Wales
Campaigners and women previously convicted of illegal abortions have hailed a “historic day” after the pardoning of every woman who has faced criminal investigation for ending a pregnancy during the last 150 years.
A vote in the House of Lords earlier this year introduced legislation to pardon women accused of terminating their own pregnancies outside the legal framework and expunge their criminal records, under section 242 of the Crime and Policing Act 2026, which takes effect on Monday.
The House of Commons had previously voted to amend the laws around abortion to prevent future cases of women being criminalised for ending their own pregnancies, while keeping the legal framework for terminations in place.
However, some women have said that while they are “grateful” for the pardon, they would also like a formal apology from the government, as “none of us should have been on trial, investigated or sent to prison”.
It is understood that the pardons will apply to about 150 women, who have been identified from police records.
Details of convictions, cautions, arrests and police investigations relating to terminations will now be deleted from the women’s records, allowing them to work and travel without restrictions once more.
Several women were prosecuted after ordering medication online or obtaining drugs after a remote consultation, including during the Covid-19 pandemic, to terminate their pregnancies.
Some have spoken publicly about not realising they were beyond 24 weeks at the time including Nicola Packer, who was cleared by a jury at Isleworth crown court in London last year after an almost five-year ordeal.
She was prosecuted after she obtained pills from an authorised provider at the height of the pandemic, and had not realised that her pregnancy was more advanced than she initially thought.
Some of the women who have advocated for a change in the law were victims of domestic abuse or coercive control, including Laura*, a young mother who was jailed after her abusive partner coerced her into obtaining pills online.
“We’ve all been through so much to get here,” Packer said. “Although it can’t erase the memories of what we’ve experienced, it does remove the records that have made it difficult for some of us to get and keep jobs, and live our lives.”
“And it further validates the feeling that none of us should have been on trial, investigated or sent to prison,” she added. “It’s a great day for us and I feel lighter knowing that the records have been expunged.”
Amy* said she was “grateful” for the pardon, though it did not “undo the years of stigma, distress and judgment”. She said women had their parenting questioned, faced restrictions on contact with their own children and were seen as “a serious danger to society”.
“I do believe women deserved an apology for what they went through,” she said. “Although the authorities may have been acting within the law at the time, we have to remember that for many women, particularly during Covid, there was isolation, fear and nowhere to turn.
“Women were dealing with incredibly difficult circumstances, often without the support or help they needed.”
She added: “For me, the hardest part is knowing that I will always carry this experience with me. The publicity surrounding my case meant that my identity and where I lived became public knowledge.
“People know who I am and where I live, and even now I can struggle to walk into my local community without feeling that people are looking at me or judging me. Having a pardon doesn’t take away those experiences or give me back the privacy I lost.”
Up until the recent law change, women were often prosecuted under Victorian legislation dating back to 1861. They include Fanny Warboys, who was criminalised a year later, in 1862, a widow who ended up injured after a backstreet abortion and was sentenced to three months in prison.
after newsletter promotion
Another woman, Mary Jane Baynon, 32, was jailed for three months in 1891 after travelling to London from her home in Sligo in western Ireland, and being reported to police by a fake surgeon.
In an early example of judges showing compassion for women who found themselves before the courts, Emma Sarah Rice, 25, was found guilty of an illegal abortion, but was sentenced to just one day without hard labour in 1881. She was still pregnant and in ill health, and “his Lordship said he thought the woman was more to be pitied than condemned”.
Dr Alison Wright, the president of the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RCOG), said the pardons recognised “the injustice of historical convictions” and she was “delighted to see this progress”.
Dr Jonathan Lord, the co-chair of the RCOG’s abortion taskforce, welcomed a “historic day”, when “for the first time since the 13th century, women who have been convicted after a pregnancy loss for an alleged abortion will no longer have to carry the consequences of a criminal record”.
Many of the women prosecuted had no other convictions or cautions, but found themselves unable to work in certain jobs because they had been arrested for abortion offences.
Others found themselves having to disclose traumatic medical events to potential employers, even though they were never charged with a crime, as their arrests had shown on enhanced Disclosure and Barring Service checks.
Heidi Stewart, the chief executive of the British Pregnancy Advisory Service (BPAS), said: “For too long, women have faced the devastating consequences of outdated abortion laws … While no pardon can undo the distress and trauma these women have experienced, this historic change in the law recognises the profound harm caused by their criminalisation and represents a meaningful step towards justice.”
Women affected do not need to apply to have their convictions removed, or take any action, as police forces and courts will begin updating records in line with new requirements, which the government has described as “a priority”.
Alex Davies-Jones, the minister for victims and tackling violence against women and girls, said: “Pardoning women for abortion offences related to their own pregnancy has been a priority and I’m pleased to be able to commence the change that parliament voted for.
“For those affected, I know that clear and accessible information about what happens next is vital. Women do not have to take any direct action themselves, but can find out more information online and contact our dedicated casework team.”

articles.title_orig: Helen Haines: Australian MP 'full of gratitude' upon leaving hospital after alleged car attack
articles.title_zh: Helen Haines: Australian MP 'full of gratitude' upon leaving hospital after alleged car attack
articles.content_orig:
Australian politician Helen Haines has said she is "full of gratitude" upon being discharged from hospital, four weeks after she was allegedly attacked with a car and left a double amputee.
The independent MP was struck outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, north-east of Melbourne, on October 19, an incident which horrified Australia.
Brendan Nugent, 43, has been charged with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and the federal offence of causing harm to a public official. He has yet to enter pleas.
In her first public comments since the attack, Haines, 65, said she had moved into the rehabilitation stage of her recovery.
"This is a really positive moment, and I am full of gratitude for the expert and compassionate care I received at the Alfred and am receiving in this next stage," Haines said.
"I appreciate the thousands of warm wishes and supportive messages from people across Indi, throughout Australia and around the world. They are giving me strength as I focus on this next phase of healing."
She added that she had been "overwhelmed" by the generosity of well wishers who had donated to Save the Children in her honour.
Haines, known for supporting stronger climate action and helping establish a national anti-corruption commission, entered parliament in 2019 as the Member for Indi after working as a nurse and midwife.
Victoria Police has said its investigation, with support from the Australian Federal Police, remains ongoing and a motive is yet to be established.
Nugent's father said he and his wife had been long-time friends of Haines, and Nugent's lawyer has said his client has mental health concerns.
The incident sparked a reckoning in the country more broadly over the tone of public debate.
Though a motive is still unclear, politicians, law enforcement, and experts have said heated public discourse is heightening the threat of political violence in the country.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said he had been in regular contact with Haines and her "extraordinary" family.
"All our thoughts and prayers continue to be with Helen for her recovery," he said in a statement.
"We continue to provide support to Helen, her family, community and staff as she undertakes her rehabilitation."

articles.title_orig: Apple launches an AI health tool as part of a research study - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Apple launches an AI health tool as part of a research study - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
Users will be able to ask the study app personalized health questions.
Artificial intelligence chatbots are becoming popular tools for people seeking information about their health. But so are headlines about possibly incorrect or even harmful information.
On Sunday, Apple announced a new approach, launching the Apple Health AI Usage Study app that they say will answer health questions only using trusted medical research and based on your health metrics and records -- if you choose to allow it.
The study hopes to evaluate user trust, how well information is understood, how helpful the information is and how much it helps patients interact with their doctors.
"It’s important to create interactions that are responsible, easy to understand, and can help someone navigate traditional care,” Dr. Sumbul Desai, Apple's vice president of Health and Fitness, told ABC News. "When people have access to clear, medically grounded information, they can walk into their doctor’s appointments feeling more prepared, informed, and confident. Rigorously studying these experiences is essential to ensuring AI serves as a bridge, not a barrier, to better care.”
Users will be able to ask the study app everyday health questions and see linked, peer-reviewed clinical citations -- showing users where the advice is coming from.
Apple is collaborating with OpenEvidence, an AI tool that is used by doctors and is trained on sources like medical journals that may not be available to other AI platforms.
Full access to OpenEvidence is currently only available to health care professionals and returns answers in a language that they are used to.
Apple says they are using their own technology to turn that research into easy-to-understand answers.
According to a February 2026 Oxford study published in Nature Medicine, AI chatbots accurately identify medical conditions nearly 95% of the time when tested on clinical cases, yet everyday users reach the right answer less than 35% of the time when trying to understand dense guidance. Yet 35% of adults, or about half of adults under 30, are already using AI chatbots, according to the Pew Research Center.
“Millions of people are turning to AI for health advice, but accurate answers aren’t always useful. Confusing or incomplete information can create false reassurance or delay care. We need to understand how people actually use these tools,” said Dr. John Brownstein, professor of pediatrics and biomedical informatics at Harvard Medical School and an ABC News contributor.
Users who sign up for the study can also choose to share or not share data that they may already have on their phone's health app, such as resting heart rate, activity, sleep, or blood test results, to get more personalized responses.
The study will also explore how health AI can potentially help participants better prepare for clinical visits with their own doctors and will ask the user for feedback along the way about how the experience is going. For example, someone asking how to improve their resting heart rate could receive advice based on their own health measurements, rather than general recommendations.
“We're collecting enormous amounts of personal health data through phones and wearables, but turning that information into something people can actually understand and act on remains a challenge,” Brownstein said.
Another part of the research is finding out whether users understand the answers they receive. Participants can rate the answers they receive and complete occasional surveys to share their experiences.
“We need to understand not just whether AI provides accurate answers, but whether people understand those answers, trust them appropriately and ultimately make better health decisions,” Brownstein said.
What about privacy and safety?
Apple says questions are processed through privacy protections designed to remove identifying information before reaching OpenEvidence.
OpenEvidence will delete question-and-response data within 24 hours and not train its model on the queries, according to Apple. The app also includes safeguards intended to recognize potentially dangerous situations and encourage users to seek professional medical assistance.
Apple emphasizes that the study does not provide live medical monitoring or replace a healthcare professional, and the app will make that clear while using it.
The study is open to U.S. adults ages 21 and older who have an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone (iPhone 15 Pro or later) running iOS 26 or later.
Participants can download the dedicated study app and complete an informed consent process. You can download the study app to learn more about the study and choose to enroll.
Apple told ABC News the goal of this research project is not just to inform their future products, but they plan to make the research available broadly to help the future of computer-assisted health communication.

articles.title_orig: Apple launches new app to study how people use AI for health
articles.title_zh: Apple launches new app to study how people use AI for health
articles.content_orig:
Big AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic have made their bets on offering chatbots that can answer health-related queries with specialized features. Apple is debuting a new study to understand how people use AI for health. But it isn’t quite following other AI startups just yet; it wants to study how clinically grounded answers can help people.
The iPhone maker is partnering with healthcare-focused AI company OpenEvidence to launch a new study app. Apple is inviting users in the U.S. over 21, using iPhone 15 or later, and running iOS 26 or later, with Apple Intelligence enabled. The company is aiming to run this study with up to 200,000 participants for more than 12 months.
The new app will allow users to ask health-related questions, as they do with ChatGPT or Claude, with answers grounded in clinical data, from sources including The New England Journal of Medicine, Journal of the American Medical Association, and Nature. Apple said that the app will try to give simplified answers to everyday medical questions. Users can rate those answers and provide feedback about the responses; they’ll also be asked to participate in monthly surveys.
Participants can share data from HealthKit such as resting heart rate, activity, sleep, or lab results to get more personalized and pointed suggestions from the app. The company said the app can also help prepare participants better for a doctor’s visit, and it will guide users to specific providers for answers related to concerning medical issues.
Apple specified that the data will be anonymized before sending it to a secure third-party cloud provider, and it won’t be used to train any kind of AI models. The company said that OpenEvidence deletes the query and response data after 24 hours.
“At Apple, we believe responsible innovation starts with scientific rigor and clinical grounding. Health is deeply personal, and conducting a dedicated research study is the most thoughtful way to understand how people engage with, comprehend, and evaluate health AI in everyday life,” Sumbul Desai, M.D., Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness, said in a statement, adding, “Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey.”
The app is available to download starting today for U.S. users. It’s not clear if Apple wants to release AI-powered answering to its Health app or Siri yet. The potential is huge — earlier this year, OpenAI said users were asking over 300 million health-related queries each week .

articles.title_orig: Thousands of US flights cancelled or delayed two days after grounding of planes nationwide
articles.title_zh: Thousands of US flights cancelled or delayed two days after grounding of planes nationwide
articles.content_orig:
Thousands of US flights were cancelled or delayed on Sunday as the US air-traffic control system continued to recover from a technical failure that led to a rare national ground stop.
Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said normal operations may not be restored until Monday.
"We have airplanes and crews that are out of position, so it takes a little bit of time," he told the BBC's US partner CBS. More than 8,800 flights were delayed and 2,400 cancelled on Sunday.
President Donald Trump urged Congress on Sunday to approve more money to modernise the air-traffic control system. The grounding of all aircraft scheduled to depart the US on Friday caused chaos at airports across the country.
More than 3,500 airplanes were in the air when the FAA announced at 15:54 EST (20:54 GMT) that flights would be grounded until further notice. Some were diverted to other airports and others flew on to their destinations.
In the aftermath, 8,500 flights were delayed and another 8,000 cancelled, according to FlightAware.
The stoppage left passengers stuck inside planes on the tarmac, unable to take off or to return to their gates. Others were stranded in airports, sleeping on the floor and desperately trying to get in touch with their airline. The ground stop also had a knock-on effect on schedules around the world, with some flights out of the UK and Europe cancelled.
The ground stop was lifted after about four and a half hours, but the impacts continued over the weekend.
On Saturday, airlines cancelled more than 5,900 flights and more than 7,000 others were delayed.
Investigators are still working to determine the root cause and who is at fault, but Duffy said the administration decided to ground flights after failures in a key system that allows air traffic controllers and pilots to communicate.
The transport secretary said a computer router installed as part of an upgrade from copper wire to fibre started sending out faulty signals.
He said on Sunday that the router - a piece of equipment which directs traffic across the network - was installed in El Dorado, Arkansas, and "flooded our network".
Duffy said that issues will continue to arise until the US makes major modernising changes to its air control system. The system needs a complete overhaul, he said.
"Let's not lie to each other," he said on NBC's Meet The Press. "We have to make investments into a network that has been neglected for decades."
In a post on Truth Social on Sunday, Trump urged US lawmakers to allocate the money, saying "we can get it built quickly and efficiently".
"It will be the BEST SYSTEM anywhere in the World. Much of our current air control system is 50 years old - RIDICULOUS! We have already started the work, but it should be done all at once, not in drips and drabs," he said.
Experts say the US uses antiquated technology for flight communications.
Aviation analyst Miles O'Brien described the US system as "a house that's about to be condemned".
He told the BBC: "I think most of us could look at this and go 'this is a system in the United States that we have allowed to decay'. It is worse than a fixer-upper."

articles.title_zh: Saudi-Backed Forces Retreat in Yemen, Leaving Key Strait in Houthi Control
articles.content_orig:
Forces backed by Saudi Arabia in Yemen said on Sunday that they were withdrawing from the country’s Red Sea coast, where they have been fighting for weeks to retake strategic territory from the Iran-aligned Houthi militia.
A group of fighters called the Southern Armed Forces, who are allied with the government of Yemen, said in a statement that they were “redeploying” to protect the interim capital, Aden, citing recent battlefield developments and “threats targeting” the city.
Aden has been the seat of the internationally recognized government for more than a decade, since the Houthis seized control of Sanaa, the Yemeni capital.
The retreat is a blow for the Yemeni government and Saudi Arabia as the balance of power in Yemen continues to tilt toward the Houthis, analysts said.
“The Houthis are very determined to go to Aden,” said Ahmed Nagi, a senior analyst for Yemen at the International Crisis Group. “They don’t want to see any area controlled by the government or the Saudi side, so they want to take over everything at this moment.”

articles.title_orig: Bessent Says Nvidia Needs ‘Dramatic Shakeup’ With Huang Out
articles.title_zh: Bessent Says Nvidia Needs ‘Dramatic Shakeup’ With Huang Out
articles.content_orig:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday called for a "dramatic shakeup" at Nvidia after CEO Jensen Huang 's resignation, questioning whether the chipmaker pursued illicit sales of its advanced artificial intelligence chips to boost earnings.
Bessent said Nvidia's board should look outside the company for its next chief executive and suggested other executives should face scrutiny over the chip giant's compliance with U.S. export controls.
"I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?" Bessent said in an interview on Fox News.
The remarks come amid a growing feud between Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over the suspected diversion of advanced AI chips to China, even as the Treasury secretary continues to defend President Donald Trump's handling of the matter.
Both Bessent and Lutnick are expected to accompany Trump to China this week, Semafor reported Sunday, putting the two Cabinet secretaries alongside the president as he prepares to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the APEC summit.
A White House official told Reuters on Thursday that the president maintains "complete confidence" in Lutnick, despite mounting scrutiny of the secretary’s handling of the Nvidia matter.
Huang resigned Thursday following revelations about his relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed , whom U.S. intelligence officials suspect of spying for China. Megaspeed is suspected of diverting Nvidia chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls.
Nvidia named Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress interim CEO.
Bessent suggested Sunday that Nvidia's problems extended well beyond Huang.
"If this were a bank and they hadn't complied like this, the OCC would be in there right now, and a lot of the executives would be removed," Bessent said, referring to the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency.
Bessent also questioned Nvidia's financial disclosures, pointing to a surge in reported Singapore revenue as its China sales fell.
Nvidia stopped separately reporting Singapore revenue in November 2025, saying a new methodology based on customers' headquarters rather than billing addresses better reflected the geographic distribution of its sales.
Bessent's remarks came two days after he told CNBC's "Squawk Box" that several federal agencies had supported adding Megaspeed to the government's export blacklist for months.
"But Commerce has the pen," Bessent said.
The public rebuke followed reporting by Axios that Bessent confronted Lutnick in the White House Situation Room over Commerce's failure to act against Megaspeed. Commerce denied that the confrontation took place.
Lutnick is also facing scrutiny over his family's financial ties to Nvidia. CNBC reported Friday that Cantor Fitzgerald, the Wall Street firm formerly run by Lutnick and now led by his sons, has helped arrange billions of dollars in financing for Nvidia's business partners.
Cantor said Nvidia share holdings fell nearly 50% over six months as national security concerns surrounding Huang escalated. The positions were associated with client swap transactions, not proprietary investments, the investment bank said.
There is no evidence Lutnick shared sensitive information with his sons or that Cantor traded on such information.
Bessent on Sunday said Trump had drawn a firm line against sales of chips more advanced than Nvidia's H200 to China . Trump himself authorized H200 sales to approved Chinese customers in December —following months of lobbying by Huang — in an arrangement under which the U.S. government would receive a 25% cut.
Bessent's latest criticism comes two days before Nvidia is scheduled to report its first quarterly earnings since Huang's departure.

During his official visit to China in May, Trump invited Huang to attend the summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The New York Times reported that the President insisted on inviting Huang to join the delegation despite concerns over Huang’s relationship with a woman who is believed to be a Chinese spy.
Speaking with reporters on Monday, Trump repeatedly downplayed Huang’s alleged affair, insisting that he believed the tech billionaire’s assertion that he knew nothing about the alleged espionage operation.
“I really believe him,” Trump told reporters during the White House press conference. “I think that he’ll be in good shape.”

articles.title_orig: Houthis claim missile attack on Riyadh airport
articles.title_zh: Houthis claim missile attack on Riyadh airport
articles.content_orig:
Yemeni forces fighting for the internationally recognized Saudi-backed government said on Sunday that they were withdrawing from an area overlooking the strategic Bab el Mandeb strait, leaving the Iran-aligned Houthis in control.
The government’s retreat ​from the Bab el Mandeb area hands the Houthis greater leverage over the maritime choke point, creating ‌a potent pressure point on global shipping while Iran continues to disrupt traffic through the Strait of Hormuz on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula.
This dual squeeze would further isolate Gulf oil producers from their main shipping routes.
The Bab el Mandeb strait is one ​of the world’s most important and busiest routes for global seaborne commodity and goods shipments, particularly ​from Asia to Europe via Egypt’s Suez Canal.
The southern Yemeni forces said they were ⁠redeploying toward Aden, where the government is based, as the Houthis — who control much of the north, ​including the capital Sanaa and Yemen’s most populous areas — increase pressure on the southern areas still under government control.
“The Southern ​Armed Forces announce the implementation of a redeployment operation for its forces from Dhubab Airport and the Bab el Mandeb area, west of Taiz Governorate,” the southern forces said in a statement.
“This step is taken based on the priority of securing the ​capital, Aden, and the neighbouring governorates, as well as strengthening the front lines and addressing existing threats.”
Government ​forces launched a military campaign in October to recapture the strategic coastal areas from the powerful militia, which had pushed south ‌in September ⁠in an attempt to seize control of Yemen’s entire Red Sea coast. The lightning offensive brought the Houthis within reach of Bab el Mandeb.
The escalation in fighting, which broke a 2022 U.N.-brokered truce, became another volatile front in the wider U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, as the Houthis continue to launch attacks on Saudi Arabia, a key U.S. ​ally and the world’s biggest ​crude exporter.
Houthi attacks on ⁠the kingdom, which had enjoyed relative calm during the early months of the 9-month-old Iran war, have disrupted flights and oil supplies as the Houthis struck Saudi ​ports, airports and facilities of state oil company Saudi Aramco — including the kingdom’s Red Sea oil ​export hub ⁠of Yanbu.
In response, Saudi Arabia struck Houthi targets in Yemen, a country mired in civil war since 2014, when the Houthis pushed the government south. Impoverished Yemen has been grappling with one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.
Fighting ⁠is intensifying ​around the western region of Taiz, with humanitarian conditions worsening. The ​city, which hosts about half of the 300,000 people displaced across Yemen by the latest fighting, remains besieged. Aid supplies are unable to ​enter, and civilians are unable to leave.

Eight people have been detained after allegedly attempting an arson attack on the company overnight on Saturday, authorities say. No one was injured.
Estonian security services say the attempted attack was carried out on the orders of Russia’s military intelligence service, the GRU.
“If Russia continues its hybrid operations in Estonia, and we know that Russian intelligence services exploit border crossings to exert influence over people, we must be prepared to reduce the risks we face,” Prime Minister Kristen Michal said in a statement Sunday.
“Closing the border would reduce the threat to people in Estonia and send a clear message that attacks on Estonia’s defense industry and defense capabilities are unacceptable,” he added.
Border crossings will be closed from December 1, and Michal did not say when they would reopen.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova told Russian state news agency TASS that the move is part of a wider pattern of “Russophobia.”
“We’ll check all this for veracity,” Zakharova said. “But if these are their real plans, then they’re part of another bout of aggressive and unbridled Russophobia.”
Estonia’s Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said the “attempted sabotage” this weekend was “yet another reminder that Russia’s hostile activities extend far beyond Ukraine” and that “hostile actions must have consequences.” He said he expected further sanctions to be adopted targeting Russian individuals and entities at a meeting of foreign affairs ministers in Brussels, Belgium on Monday.
Ukraine has commended Estonia for its move to close the border, hailing it as an example of effective action against Russian hostility and encouraging Europe to take note.
“Estonia has shown that Russian sabotage can and should have consequences beyond diplomatic condemnation,” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said in a post on X . “This approach deserves wider support across Europe.”
Russia has long been accused of carrying out sabotage and other hybrid attacks against Europe but has repeatedly denied the claims.
Russia is escalating its attacks on Europe. The risk of a misstep is growing every day
Back in September, European officials pointed the finger at the Kremlin following a series of incidents that appeared to target NATO members.
A railway line on which several former Western diplomats were traveling was struck by a Russian drone near Ukraine’s border with Poland, while another drone – likely of Russian origin – was shot down in Lithuania. A third drone also washed ashore in Poland.
Elsewhere, a Danish helicopter was narrowly missed by a Russian flare, and Dutch rail traffic was significantly disrupted after metal pipes that had been fitted across the tracks triggered short circuits, turned traffic signals to red and forced trains to an inconvenient stop.
Despite denying involvement, Moscow has remained the alleged culprit. European NATO-member allies have deemed the actions an escalation of conflict against the bloc – characterizing the attacks as measures designed to antagonize without triggering all-out war.
